🗒️What This Means For You
  • Fed Hike: Since the 2026-09-16 Fed hike the Treasury-rate leg of IG returns is -1.25% (intraday, 7-year +18bp). At trading day 18 (last close) it was -1.25% against a five-campaign average of -1.34% at the same point — 1994-95, 2022-23 were worse. The spread leg adds -0.28%. The 10-year is +22bp since the hike vs a +18bp campaign average at the same point. The 2s10s steepening may be topping (intraday 4 of 4 signals: topping likely).
  • HY Contagion: Junk-bond stress: the CCC-to-single-B spread gap is 719bp against a five-year average of 410bp (widest since Apr 2020). Better-rated junk is following: single-B +38bp and BB +35bp in a month. CCC and single-B are moving together more (correlation 0.21 → 0.52 over 3 months; five-year norm 0.70). Investment grade is untouched (+2bp).
  • Stocks: The S&P was nearly flat, tech fell, and the Dow and Europe rose.
  • FX: The dollar firmed and the euro stays weak, trading below its recent averages.
  • Technicals: US stocks are well above their trend lines, so they're stretched but haven't broken down.
  • Sectors: Money moved into energy, staples and utilities and out of tech this week.
  • Credit/Spreads: Most bond risk premiums are still cheap, but the worst junk bonds are cracking.
  • Crisis: Stress is moderate, driven by the Iran war, high yields and weak junk bonds.
  • Inflation: Core inflation is slowly easing, but energy-driven prices are still rising fast.
  • Tech Bubble: Valuations are well below 2000 levels, but investors look complacent and credit is loose.
  • Earnings & IPOs: JPMorgan opens bank earnings Tuesday. US IPOs are quiet and India's are busy.
  • Iran: Talks have stalled and tanker attacks near Hormuz are rising, which keeps oil high.
  • Warsh: The Fed raised rates in September and hinted that more increases may follow.
  • Week Ahead: September CPI comes Wednesday, then retail sales, then Warsh speaks late in the week.
  • Outlook: Neutral near term. Rising yields and credit cracks argue for caution over the coming months.
  • Trades: Favor oil and defensive stocks, trim stretched tech and move up in credit quality.
  • Trades Vol: 45 watchlist names screened: 23 hold long, 22 stay out
  • Treasury Liquidity: Treasury liquidity/rates-vol monitor: TLT 95/100 put skew +0.50 vol pts, Fed DKW real term premium +91bp.
  • 10Y Pattern: 10Y at 97th pctile, +6bp from the 2026 rim — still compressing, not a cup-and-handle.
  • Diesel Futures: Diesel: 1-9 of 10 signals point lower.
  • Bottom line: The surface is calm, but junk-bond stress is quietly spreading. Stay selective.

PM, Oct 12. It was a split, low-conviction Columbus Day session. The S&P 500 slipped -0.055% to 7807.24. The Nasdaq Composite fell -0.44% to 27245.9 and the Russell 2000 fell -0.45%, while the Dow rose +0.38% to 51850.55. VIX ticked up to 15.21 from 14.84. Europe did better than the US: STOXX 600 +0.65%, Euro Stoxx 50 +0.45%, FTSE 100 +0.99% to 10656.28. The Nikkei shows Friday's close because Japan was on holiday. US Treasury yields printed unchanged (2Y 4.7869%, 10Y 5.2378%, 30Y 5.5956%) because the US bond market was closed for Columbus Day (https://www.kiplinger.com/investing/economy/this-weeks-economic-calendar). Treat the flat rates and US credit prints as a holiday artifact, not as calm. The day's biggest story was oil and geopolitics. Brent rose +1.24% to 106.02 and WTI is reported +2.06% at 93.74. Iran's IRGC claimed strikes on three supertankers, the US disabled a vessel running its naval blockade, and Tehran called the latest US proposal 'insufficient' (https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/11/hormuz-attacks-intensify-as-efforts-to-end-war-on-iran-stall). Rotation followed: energy (+1.48%), staples (+1.22%) and communication services (+1.12%) led the US, while info tech (-0.90%) and discretionary (-0.73%) lagged. The more important development is under the surface in junk bonds. The Caa–B gap (the extra yield on the riskiest CCC-rated junk bonds over single-B bonds) is 719bp. That is the 100th percentile of its 5-year range, against a 5-year average near 410bp. The gap is +97bp over 1 month and +204bp over 3 months, its widest since 2020-04-24. On the ICE BofA cross-check, CCC OAS is 1252bp and the CCC–B gap is 937bp, both at the 100th percentile. Is it spreading? Partly. Single-B is +38bp over 1 month (to 295bp) and Ba is +35bp (to 189bp). The B–Ba gap has barely moved (+3bp in 1 month, 106bp, 31st percentile of its 5-year range), so the better junk grades are widening together rather than single-B breaking away. Investment grade has hardly moved (81bp, +2bp in 1 month). The correlation of daily Caa and B spread moves has risen to 0.52 from 0.28 a month ago and 0.21 three months ago, though it is still below its 5-year median of 0.70. This is a descriptive pattern, not a validated signal. Sentiment: index-level calm sits over defensive rotation, higher oil and widening lower-quality credit, with Wednesday's September CPI (headline seen 3.6% YoY) and Fed Chair Warsh's remarks later in the week as the next tests (https://investinglive.com/news/week-ahead-us-inflation-and-retail-sales-lead-a-busy-economic-calendar-be-aware/).

Two-sided analog episodes per signal: days where the signal's percentile-rank (vs its own full history) was <=5th or >=95th, or |z-score|>=1.3, clustered into one episode per zone per >=6-month gap between episode starts. For each zone, the realized forward 6-month % change in the BENCHMARK'S OUTRIGHT PRICE from each episode start is measured; a card's direction (BUY/SELL) is whichever sign that median historical move carries. Entry/target/stretch/stop are computed directly from this table -- the narrative prose (thesis/rationale) is the only part supplied by an LLM, and it is not permitted to alter a number. Crack spreads and curve shapes are, financially, relative-value signals rather than clean predictors of outright price; expressing every card in outright price terms is a deliberate simplification. HO36 Comdty (ULSD's 36-month point) is thin/less liquid on this seat -- treat its curve-shape reading with lower confidence than the others. Not investment advice.

Churn = the longest window of 20-120 sessions whose close range is <= 8x its median ATR(14), with median ADX(14) < 20, an insignificant close-price slope (p > 0.05), and >= 2 entries into each edge zone (top/bottom 20% of the band). Support/resistance = median swing low/high (+/-5 sessions); outer edges = the window's extreme closes. Breakout = a close beyond the outer edge by > 0.5 ATR, confirmed by a second close or one close beyond 1 ATR. A break back inside within 5 sessions is a failed break. An episode's outer edges can widen at most 0.5 ATR past their first detection, so a slow grind can't drag the range along with it. Base rates come from replaying the same rules over the full history, day by day, with no lookahead. This is pattern analysis of historical prices, not investment advice.

Single-B (295bp, +38bp in 1 month) and Ba (189bp, +35bp in 1 month) are widening together, and HY–IG is 229bp (+37bp in 1 month). IG is barely moving (81bp). The Caa/B correlation rose to 0.52 from 0.21 three months ago (5-year median 0.70). This is descriptive, not a validated signal. Key levels (analyst framing): HY OAS returning to its 5-year B/Ba averages (B ~348bp, Ba ~219bp) would mean the stress has broadened into mainstream junk. IG moving up toward its 5-year average (~102bp) would need a growth or earnings scare, such as a weak bank-earnings read on credit costs. On the downside, the CCC gap narrowing back toward its ~410bp 5-year average would need a Hormuz de-escalation and a softer CPI.

💧Treasury liquidity & rates volcomputed

US Govt Securities Liquidity Index (GVLQUSD), MOVE, Fed DKW term premium and TLT option skew, live from Bloomberg + federalreserve.gov.

Five charts tracking the mechanism Simon White laid out for why Treasury liquidity is deteriorating: rising inflation volatility feeds into a higher term premium, which steepens the curve, which raises bond vol, which shows up as worse UST market liquidity. Right now UST liquidity is at the 48th percentile of its own history (higher = worse) and the Fed's own DKW real term premium is +91bp.

Latest reading is +0.50 vol points (5th percentile of the 40 runs recorded so far). Positive means the 5%-OTM put is pricier than the at-the-money option -- the market paying up for downside-price / higher-yield insurance on long-end Treasuries.

UST liquidity index is 1.51 (48th percentile of its own 2007-present history -- 100th = worst liquidity on record), deteriorating over the past 3 months (+0.05 pts). CPI YoY volatility (2yr) is 0.49pp; the article's thesis is that rising inflation vol drags liquidity worse, which this chart is built to let you check month to month.

Real term premium is +91bp (96th percentile of its own 2007-present history), up 12bp over the trailing ~2 months. Inflation risk premium is +14bp. Fed staff's own DKW decomposition (D'Amico-Kim-Wei, updated Kim-Walsh-Wei) splits the rise in long yields into a policy-uncertainty component (real term premium) and an inflation-uncertainty component -- both rising is the article's read that this move isn't just a rate-expectations story.

MOVE is 98.5 (71th percentile of its own post-2007 history). The 3m10s curve is 108bp (steeper by 31bp over 3 months). The article's claim is mechanical, not just correlated -- a steeper curve gives forward rates more room to move before converging to spot, which is itself higher realized/implied vol.

MOVE and the UST liquidity index have moved together with a full-history correlation of +0.72 (both series read as 'worse' when they rise). That's the closing link in the article's chain: inflation vol -> term premium -> curve steepness -> bond vol -> liquidity.

Recreates 5 charts from Bloomberg MacroScope, 'Treasury Market Liquidity Is a Live Issue Again' (Simon White, 19-Aug-2026). TLT skew accumulates one point per report run -- Bloomberg's option-surface field is snapshot-only, not retrievable historically via the API. Term premium is the Fed's own DKW model series (D'Amico-Kim-Wei, updated Kim-Walsh-Wei), pulled directly from federalreserve.gov, not Bloomberg. Not a trading signal -- a liquidity/vol monitor only.

Retracement of the left-rim decline: 76% (needs ≥90% to pass). 10Y level that passes: 6.16% (92bp above today).
Retracement = (right rim − cup base) / (left rim − cup base) = (5.30 − 0.51) / (6.79 − 0.51) = 76%.
Pass level = cup base + 0.90 × (left rim − cup base) = 0.51 + 0.90 × (6.79 − 0.51) = 6.16%.

Same test on each trailing window: cup base = lowest close in the window, left rim = highest close before it, right rim = highest close after it. Cup complete at ≥90% retracement; above 110% the yield has run past the old high (a breakout, not a cup). No cup inside the window when its left rim is not the highest close of the 91 days before it, i.e. yields were already falling into the window. Pass level = cup base + 0.90 × (left rim − cup base).

🗞️Street View — Where the Cycle Is HeadingCURATED · AS OF 2026-10-01

⚠ Commentary is 11 days old (as of 2026-10-01); it may not reflect the latest Fed news.

Consensus is a short, shallow campaign: one or two more 25bp hikes, December more likely than October. The debate is whether hiking into an energy shock ends in recession, and the bond market is already doing some of the tightening.

The Fed

  • Sept 16: unanimous 25bp hike to 3.75–4.00%, the first since 2023. Dots: median one more hike in 2026; 16 of 18 see at least one, 4 see two. Inflation not back at 2% until 2029. (CNBC, FedAndMarkets)
  • Warsh's message was distinctly hawkish (inflation 'too high and broad-based'); the Conference Board calls it 'not a one and done'. (Conference Board)
  • Sept 29, Williams (NY Fed): 'no need for urgency'; one more hike 'late this year' may be appropriate; the biggest inflation shocks have passed. (Bloomberg, NY Fed)
  • Sept 30, August PCE came in soft: headline 3.4% (vs 3.7% expected), core 3.0% (vs 3.3%). October odds fell; December still priced. Kashkari: inflation 'still too high'. (CNBC, CNBC (Kashkari))

Market pricing

  • October 28 hike odds vary widely by venue, roughly 35% to 69% (prediction markets highest, CME futures ~58%), mostly measured before the soft PCE print. (PredictionMarketsPicks)
  • About 83% odds of another hike by year-end; futures price ~93bp of tightening over the next 9 meetings, more than the dots. (Forbes)

Bonds and credit

  • 10-year Treasury above 5.25% (Sept 28), the highest since 2007; 30-year ~5.49%. Drivers cited: sticky energy inflation (Iran war), heavy issuance, AI capex demand. Term premium ~1.0–1.4%. (CNBC, CNBC (Warsh's yield problem))
  • AI-related issuers trade ~115bp vs ~78bp for IG overall; high-yield AI supply $40B year to date vs $12B in all of 2025. BNP and Goldman warn the issuance could pressure spreads. (Reuters, Bloomberg (BNP))

The bear case

  • Rosenberg: the Fed has never hiked into an energy shock without a recession, and AI won't save it this time. (TheStreet)
  • Goldman called the case for hiking 'weak' (demand not overheating, energy inflation should fade when the war ends). Oxford Economics: 'The Fed cannot control energy prices'; the risk is a weaker labor market. (CNN)

Read-through: For bonds, the bigger risk is the long end, not the Fed: term premium and supply keeping the 10-year above 5% matter more than one extra 25bp. The recession call is loud but isn't in any sell-side house view yet.

Curated summary of published Fed, market and economist commentary (news and research via the web), not a computed series and not a forecast. Odds differ by venue and move daily.

🔥Is Inflation Persistent?

Persistence score: 58/100 — Mixed and modestly sticky. Every underlying core gauge is trending lower (Median CPI 2.58, 16% Trimmed-Mean CPI 2.57, Median PCE 2.57, Trimmed-Mean PCE 2.19, Core Sticky CPI 2.70, all 'falling'), so the computed core-trend read is middling rather than alarming. Breadth and energy pass-through are the problem. In the Dallas distribution, 28.9% of the PCE basket (13.2% above 10% plus 15.7% at 5-10%) is rising faster than 5%, and Flexible CPI runs at 4.94. Core PCE at 3.00759 sits well above core CPI at 2.4. With headline September CPI expected at 3.6% YoY and oil rising, the headline will look hot while core cools only slowly. That is enough to keep the Warsh Fed leaning toward hikes.

Bubble-analog — today's Nasdaq vs the dot-com cycle (two anchors)

WHY TWO START DATES?
Each line is rebased to 100 at a low the tech bull launched from, so elapsed time lines up. Oct-2022 is today's anchor — it was the prior bear-market bottom. Oct-1990 is the dot-com cycle's equivalent (its literal prior bear bottom). But 1990 predates the internet mania by ~4 years, so the second chart re-anchors the dot-com line to the 1994 reset low, just before the surge ignited, for a tighter like-for-like. Today sits very early under the strict 1990 analog, further along under the 1994 surge analog.
━ Anchored at the prior bear-market bottom (Oct-1990)   ━ today's cycle
━ Anchored at the pre-internet reset low (1994)   ━ today's cycle

Valuation marker: today's Nasdaq P/E (43x) ≈ 24% of the ~175x 2000-peak P/E.

IF THIS RHYMES WITH 2000
Nasdaq fell -78.0% peak→trough (2000-03-10 → 2002-10-09, ~31 months); it took ~15 years to reclaim the high.

The 2000 analogy works better for credit and sentiment than for valuation. Spreads and financial conditions are as loose as or looser than at the dot-com peak, and volatility is cheap. Earnings-multiple stretch, however, is a fraction of the 1999-2000 mania, outside semiconductors. Now that the Fed is hiking (first hike since 2023 in September) and the 10Y is above 5.2%, the usual late-cycle ingredients are a restrictive policy turn and widening credit, and the CCC tail is already widening. A 2000-style top would need either a final melt-up in multiples or a broadening credit break. Neither is complete. The five numbers above (top-10 concentration, IPO froth, CAPE, market-cap/GDP, LT EPS-growth expectations) are analyst estimates. They were NOT verified by web search this run, so treat them as approximate.

⚔️Iran War

The war is in a stalled-diplomacy, escalating-at-sea phase. Iran's IRGC claimed on Monday to have struck three supertankers over two days. The US military said Sunday it disabled a cargo vessel that tried to run the US naval blockade. Tehran called Washington's latest proposal 'insufficient'. Trump says he rejected an Iranian offer to reopen Hormuz, though Iran's foreign minister says Tehran has not formally responded. No breakthrough is expected before the Nov 3 US midterms (Al Jazeera, Oct 11). CBS reports Trump has promised not to resume strikes before the midterms. A week of Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia's main airport has killed at least 20 people, including a US national, and Trump is weighing joining Saudi-led strikes in Yemen. The US sanctioned 17 'shadow fleet' vessels Thursday, and the Pentagon puts the war's cost at at least $33.4 billion. Market read: tanker attacks plus the blockade keep a risk premium in crude (Brent 106.02), which feeds headline inflation and the Fed's hawkish lean. These reports span roughly Oct 9–12. Exact datelines for some items could not be confirmed.

🏦Fed Chair Warsh
NEAR TERM

Next FOMC is Oct 28 (per DailyCoin's calendar). Inference: another 25bp hike, to 4.00–4.25%, is more likely than a pause. The case rests on his Jackson Hole warning that inflation was too high and hikes might be needed, the unanimous 12-0 September hike to 3.75–4.00%, and language analysts read as 'not one-and-done'. The swing factor is Wednesday's CPI (headline seen 3.6%) and his remarks late this week. This is inferred from his record, not announced.

~1 YEAR

Inference: a cumulative tightening path that takes the policy rate modestly higher over the next year (two to three more hikes is plausible if war-driven inflation persists), paired with his long-held preference for a smaller Fed balance sheet and less forward guidance. A quick reversal would most likely come from a credit or growth shock. Political friction with Trump, who wants lower rates, is a persistent overhang, but Warsh has publicly pushed back.

On record: at Jackson Hole (Aug 28) Warsh said inflation was still too high and signaled possible hikes. On Sep 16 the FOMC raised rates by 25bp, unanimously, to 3.75–4.00%, the first hike since 2023. He cited a stronger economy, inflation that didn't slow, and intensified geopolitical tensions, and framed the move as removing 'a dose of accommodation'. CNBC noted his phrasing left Wall Street wondering how far hikes will go, and markets price several more. He has bluntly rebuffed Trump's rate criticism. Flag: the near-term and one-year paths above are my inferences from these statements, not Fed guidance.
